chunks: Why multiple clock domains. The question: Why are multiple clock domains needed?
A chip is not one block ticking to one clock. A processor wants a very fast clock, and a serial port (a slow one-bit-at-a-time link) needs only a slow one.
Interfaces like USB have clocks set by standards. Separate clock domains let each part run only as fast as it needs, which saves power.
The price is that passing signals between unrelated clocks is risky and needs special circuits.
Picture a baton relay between two runners who each step to their own drumbeat.
If the first hands over the baton at a random moment, the second may fumble it, and for a moment neither holds it nor has dropped it.
A safe design hands the baton to a waiting shelf first. The second runner picks it up one full beat later, once it has settled.
Both flops are clocked by the destination clock (CLK B). FF1 samples the asynchronous input and may become metastable; the full cycle before FF2 samples gives it time to resolve.
Never put logic between FF1 and FF2.
Clock domain: a group of circuits driven by one clock, or by clocks with a fixed relationship. Flip-flop: a circuit that stores one bit, capturing its input on each clock tick.
Metastability: a flip-flop stuck between 0 and 1 for a short while, because its input changed just as it captured.
Synchronizer: two flip-flops (flops, for short) in a row that give the first one time to settle. Gray code: a counting code where each step changes only one bit.
For a single-bit signal, a synchronizer on the receiving side gives the first flop a full tick to settle before the second reads it. A multi-bit counter is trickier.
Binary 0111 (7) goes to 1000 (8), and all four bits change. If the other side samples mid-change, it may read 1111 (15), a value that never existed.
In Gray code, 7 is 0100 and 8 is 1100, so only one bit differs, and a sample is either 7 or 8. That is the whole idea.
"Different blocks need different clock rates: CPUs run at GHz, peripherals at a few MHz, an always-on timer at 32 kilohertz, and interfaces like USB or DDR have clocks set by their standards.
Separate domains let me save dynamic power, apply DVFS and clock gating per block, and keep clock trees manageable.
The price is clock domain crossing: signals between unrelated clocks can go metastable, so I use synchronizers for single bits and Gray-coded async FIFOs or handshakes for buses."
